cards.title: What Was the Industrial Revolution?
body: The Industrial Revolution was a period of major mechanization and innovation that began in Great Britain during the mid-18th century and early 19th century.
The British Industrial Revolution was dominated by the exploitation of coal and iron.

cards.title: The main points
body: *The first Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain in the 1700s and 1800s and was a time of significant innovation.
*The American Industrial Revolution followed in the late 19th century and was an engine of economic growth in the U.S.
*The Industrial Revolution led to inventions that included the assembly line, telegraph, steam engine, sewing machine, and internal combustion engine.

*Working for businesses during the Industrial Revolution paid better wages than agricultural work. The increase in the number of factories and migration to the cities led to pollution, deplorable working and living conditions, and child labor.

cards.title: How Did the Industrial Revolution Impact Society?
body: Although the Industrial Revolution occurred approximately 200 years ago, it is a period that left a profound impact on how people lived and the way businesses operated.
Arguably, the factory systems developed during the Industrial Revolution are responsible for creating capitalism and the modern cities of today.
Often the wages were low, and conditions were harsh. However, working for such businesses still paid a better living wage than farming.
Production efficiency improved during the Industrial Revolution with inventions such as the steam engine.
The steam engine dramatically reduced the time it took to manufacture products.
Before the use of coal, wood was the primary energy source; coal provided three times more energy than wood, and Britain had large coal deposits.

cards.title: Advantages of Industrialization
body: The Industrial Revolution created an increase in employment opportunities. This led to significant improvements in city planning.
Increased innovation also led to higher levels of education
made life comfortable for many though living conditions for workers remained abhorrent,
This eventually fueled the rise of labor unions that led to improved working conditions and fair wages.

cards.title: Completing this point: the good and the bad of industrialization
body: **Advantages.** (1) Europe's population nearly doubled, from 140 million in 1750 to 266 million in 1850, because food supply rose and famine largely disappeared. (2) Cities grew quickly as factories moved to them. (3) A new **industrial middle class** of factory owners, bankers and professionals appeared. (4) Cheaper goods and new inventions made life more comfortable for many.

**Disadvantages.** (1) The new **industrial working class** worked 12–16 hours a day, six days a week, with no job security and no minimum wage. (2) Mines and textile factories were unhealthy and dangerous. (3) Women and children made up two-thirds of the British cotton workforce by 1830; women were paid half or less of men's wages. (4) Crowded cities had poor housing and sanitation.
**The result.** These conditions led to labour unions, socialist ideas and, later, reforms.
**Memory trick:** "More people, more goods – but long hours and bad homes."

cards.title: Disadvantages of Industrialization
body: It led to a shortage of food production.
An increase in urban pollution.
Working conditions in factories deteriorated. Long hours, inadequate remuneration, and minimal breaks became the norm.
Child labor was a significant issue. Health issues arose for many of the factory workers giving rise to the labor movement throughout the U.S.

cards.title: Rise of socialism
body: In the first half of the 19th century, the difficult conditions created by the Industrial Revolution gave rise to a movement known as Socialism.
Socialism is a system in which society, usually in the form of the state, owns and controls the main means of production, such as factories and utilities.
Early Socialism was largely the idea of intellectuals who believed in the equality of all people and who wanted to replace competition with cooperation in industry.
To later Socialists, especially the followers of Karl Marx, such ideas were impractical dreams. The later Socialists named the earlier theorists utopian socialists.

cards.title: What Key Innovations Took Place During the Industrial Revolution? – Revolutions of 1848
body: Main topics
* Revolutions of 1848: An Overview
* Causes of the Revolutions of 1848
* Impact of the Revolutions of 1848

cards.title: Background – What did Liberal Nationalism represent?
body: ‘Liberalism’ is derived from the Latin word, meaning free. Voting and election rights were granted only to men who owned property.

cards.title: Age of Revolution 1830-1848
body: As conservative regimes tried to consolidate their power, liberalism and nationalism came to be increasingly associated with revolution in many regions of Europe such as the Italian and German states, the provinces of the Ottoman Empire, Ireland and Poland.

The first upheaval took place in France in July 1830. The Bourbon kings who had been restored to power during the conservative reaction after 1815, were now overthrown by liberal revolutionaries who installed a constitutional monarchy with Louis Philippe at its head.

cards.title: A New Conservatism after 1815
body: In 1815, European governments were driven by the spirit of conservation. The Conservatives believed in royalty, Church, civil society, and property and that the family should be preserved.
In 1815, representatives of European countries - Britain, Russia, Prussia, and Austria met in Vienna to form a concert of Europe.

The Bourbon Empire was restored to power, and France lost its lands to Napoleon. The biggest challenge taken by the liberal-nationalists, who criticized the new law-abiding system, was media freedom (free press).

cards.title: Why is 1848 called the year of revolution?
body: 1848 is called the year of revolution because revolutions broke out in multiple European countries this year. Revolutionary turmoil ricked German and Italian states, Italy, Austrian Empire, and Denmark. Most of these revolutions failed at their goal of political liberalization, however.

cards.title: Causes the Revolutions of 1848
body: The Revolutions of 1848 were caused by spread of ideas such as popular sovereignty (arguing for political liberalization of absolute monarchies), nationalism, and socialism. Their more immediate cause was economic crisis in Europe in 1845-48.

cards.title: What did the Revolutions of 1848 mean for France?
body: The revolution of 1848 was initially successful in France, abolishing a corrupt oligarchy of King Louis-Philippe and installing a democratic republic instead. However, the republic survived only two years. In 1850, it was abolished by its democratically elected president, Louis-Napoleon, nephew of Napoleon Bonaparte, who restored the French Empire.

cards.title: Revolutions of 1848: An Overview – Causes of the Revolutions of 1848
body: The revolutions of 1848 in Europe resembled a wave; they started in Sicily in January 1848 and subsequently erupted in other countries.

As mentioned, although particular causes varied across countries, the main revolutions of 1848 causes were the ideas of political liberalization, nationalism, and socialism. These ideas made people demand political change.
The more immediate cause of the revolutions was the economic crisis of 1845-47. Many European countries were struck by poor harvest and famine, making anti-government protests increasingly likely.
Revolutions of 1848: Timeline of Events

The revolutions of 1848 started in January 1848 in Sicily. After the revolution in Sicily achieved a (temporary) success by forcing the King to proclaim a constitution, protests broke out in February 1848 in France and other Italian states, and in March 1848 in the German states, the Austrian (Hapsburg) Empire, and Denmark. There were also minor protests in other countries.

cards.title: Revolutions of 1848: Sicily, Italy
body: Before the outbreak of the revolutions, Italy was divided politically. Its southern part was controlled by the Kingdom of Two Sicilies, a repressive absolute monarchy.

Papal States, governed by the Pope, occupied most of central Italy. Most of the north was controlled by the Austrian Empire, either directly or indirectly, as several smaller Italian states were ruled by branches of the Hapsburg dynasty. The Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont occupied the northwestern part of the country and the island of Sardinia.
Due to this political division, Italian revolutionaries had dual goals; political liberalization and Italian unification, the latter resulting from their nationalist views.

These goals were embraced by the King of Piedmont, who proclaimed a liberal constitution and in March 1848, attacked the Austria-controlled Lombardy to aid the anti-Austrian uprisings there. After initial setbacks, Austrians ultimately defeated Italian forces at Novara in March 1849 and restored their rule in Northern Italy. The Pope, who initially supported Italian unification, decided to withdraw his troops, leading to an uprising in Rome and creation of a democratic Roman Republic on February 9, 1849. However, a French military intervention reestablished the Pope's rule on July 3, 1849. The revolution in the Kingdom of Two Sicilies was also crushed by the King in a few months, and absolute monarchy was reintroduced there.

cards.title: The February Revolution – France
body: In contrast to Prussia and Austria, which were absolute monarchies, France, before the February Revolution of 1848, was a constitutional monarchy.

However, the French were growing dissatisfied with the rule of King Louis Philippe I, whose government grew increasingly corrupt, kept suffrage restricted to only 2% of male adults, and repressed the press.

The February Revolution began on February 23, 1848, when protests broke out in Paris following cancellation of a political meeting, leading to the King's abdication in just two days. A republic (known as the Second Republic) was proclaimed.
A workers' uprising that broke out in June 1848 in Paris was brutally crushed by the government.
In December 1848, a charismatic and populist leader, Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte (nephew of Napoleon I) was elected president with 74% of the vote.
He quickly conflicted with the legislature, which did not want to eliminate the constitutional ban on reelection.
In December 1851, Louis-Napoleon unconstitutionally dissolved the legislature, and a year later proclaimed himself the emperor following a rigged referendum.
The February Revolution ultimately resulted in the creation of another authoritarian regime, although of a populist rather than oligarchical character

cards.title: Impact of the Revolutions of 1848
body: In a short term, most Revolutions of 1848 were unsuccessful. In Austria and Italian states, absolute monarchies were introduced after the uprisings were suppressed.
France was a short-term success because it established a democratic republic, but it gave way to an autocracy in just two years.
However, the revolutions noted some success in Prussia and a few other German states, which became more liberal following the events.
Only in Denmark can the 1848 revolution be considered a clear success.

cards.title: Model answer: the Industrial Revolution
cards.problem: (Exam question) Describe the Industrial Revolution and its main results.

steps.text: Definition: a period of major mechanisation and innovation that began in Great Britain in the mid-18th century.
Basis: the British Industrial Revolution was dominated by the exploitation of coal and iron; the American Industrial Revolution followed in the late 19th century.
Inventions: the steam engine, telegraph, sewing machine, assembly line and internal combustion engine.
Results: more goods for larger markets, better transport, growth of cities and of a working class – but uneven development across the world.

cards.answer: Beginning in Britain with coal, iron and steam, the Industrial Revolution mechanised production, created new inventions and transport, and built industrial cities and a working class.

lessons.title: The Unification of Italy and Germany

cards.title: Italy Unified
body: During the middle of the nineteenth century, Italy was divided into seven states, of which only one, Sardinia-Piedmont, was ruled by an Italian princely house. Even the Italian language had not acquired one common form and still had many regional and local variations.
The failure of revolutionary uprisings both in 1831 and 1848 meant that the mantle now fell on Sardinia Piedmont under its ruler King Victor Emmanuel If to unify the Italian states through war.
Through a tactful diplomatic alliance with France engineered by Cavour, Sardinia-Piedmont succeeded in defeating the Austrian forces in 1859.
Apart from regular troops, a large number of armed volunteers under the leadership of Giuseppe Garibaldi joined the fray.

In 1860, they marched into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and succeeded in winning the support of the local peasants in order to drive out the Spanish rulers. In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy.

cards.title: Unification of Germany
body: It started with the liberal Nationalist movement of 1848 with the formation of the Frankfurt Parliament but efforts failed.
The move was then taken by Prussia and the responsibility shifted to Prime Minister Otto Von Bismarck.
Bismarck led three wars over a period of seven years with Austria, Denmark and France culminating in a Prussian victory.
Nationalist feelings were widespread among middle-class Germans, who in 1848 tried to unite the different regions of the German confederation into a nation-state governed by an elected parliament.

Prussia took on the leadership of the movement for national unification. its Chief minister, Otto von Bismarck (followed the policy of Blood and Iron), was the architect of the unification carried out with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy.
In January 1871, the Prussian king, William I was proclaimed German Emperor in a ceremony held at Versailles.

Therefore, Bismarck is the equivalent figure for Germany.

**Step 2:** So the answer is B) Ottovan Bismarck.

cards.title: Model answer: unification of Italy
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain how Italy was unified.

steps.text: Problem: Italy was divided into seven states; only Sardinia-Piedmont had an Italian ruling house, and revolts of 1831 and 1848 had failed.
Leadership: Sardinia-Piedmont under King Victor Emmanuel II and his minister Cavour.
Diplomacy and war: an alliance with France helped defeat Austria in 1859.
Volunteers: Giuseppe Garibaldi and his Red Shirts conquered the south, which joined the new Kingdom of Italy.

cards.answer: Piedmont-Sardinia, led by Victor Emmanuel II and Cavour, used French help against Austria (1859) while Garibaldi's Red Shirts won the south, creating a united Italy.

lessons.title: Europe and North America from 1850 to1914

cards.title: GREAT BRITAIN
body: Great Britain was able to avoid the Revolution in 1848. In the beginning of 19th century, Great Britain was governed by aristocratic landowning classes, which dominated both houses of Parliament.

cards.title: The changes include
body: In 1832, Parliament issued a law that increased the number of male voters.
Another reason for Britain’s stability was its continuing economic growth.
By 1871, Great Britain had a two-party parliamentary system. For the next 50 years, these two parties (the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party) were in and out of power.
By 1900 a new labor party was established
By the end of World War I (1918), all males over age 21 and women over age 30 could vote.

cards.title: France changes include
body: Four years after his election as president in 1848, Louis-Napoleon organized a plebiscite, or popular vote, for the restoration of the monarchy. A substantial majority supported the restoration and on December 2, 1852, Louis-Napoleon became Emperor of France as Napoleon III.
Napoleon III completely controlled the government and limited civil liberties but achieved economic progress

In the 1860s, opposition to some of Napoleon’s economic and governmental policies arose. In response, Napoleon III began to liberalize his regime. Soon after the French defeat in the Franco- Prussian War, however, his empire collapsed.
In 1875, five years after it was proclaimed, the Third Republic gained a republican constitution.

The new government had a president and a legislature made up of two houses. Members of the upper house, called the Senate, were elected indirectly. In the lower house, called the Chamber of Deputies, members were elected by universal male suffrage.

cards.title: The Austrian Empire – Changes include
body: After the Hapsburg rulers crushed the revolutions of 1848 and 1849, they restored centralized, autocratic government to the empire.
But after Austria’s defeat at the hands of the Prussians in 1866. The result was the Compromise of 1867. This Compromise created the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary.
The two states tied together by a single monarch, and a common army, foreign policy, and system of finances.
Thus, in domestic affairs the Hungarians had become independent.

cards.title: Germany
body: The Constitution of the new imperial Germany begun by Otto von Bismarck in 1871 provided for a two-house legislature. The lower house of the German parliament, the Reichstag, was elected on the basis of universal male suffrage.
By the reign of William II, emperor from 1888 to 1918, Germany had become the strongest military and industrial power in Europe.

cards.title: Russia
body: The Russian czar was still regarded as a divine-right monarch with unlimited power. In 1856, the Russians suffered a humiliating defeat in the Crimean War.
In order to cope with western powers, Czar Alexander II decided to make reforms. Serfdom was the largest problem in Russia.
On March 3, 1861, Alexander issued an Emancipation Proclamation, which freed the serfs. Some conservators did not like the change made. When a group of radicals assassinated Alexander II
In 1881, his son and successor, Alexander III came to power. He abandoned his father’s reform programs and returned to the old methods of repression.

In 1894 Nicholas II began his rule as a czar of Russia. Industrialization began late in Russia but progressed rapidly after 1890. By 1900, Russia had become the fourth largest producer of steel behind.
Growing dissatisfaction and opposition to the czarist regime finally gave rise to the Revolution of 1905.

On January 22, 1905, workers marched to the Winter Palace in St. Petersburg to present a petition of grievances to the czar. Troops opened fire on the peaceful demonstration, killing hundreds. This became known as “Bloody Sunday.” The massacre caused workers throughout Russia to call strikes and led to the Revolution of 1905.

The Revolution was defeated. But Nicholas II was forced to allow civil liberties and create a legislative assembly, called the Duma. These reforms, however, were short-lived. By 1907, the czar had already restricted the power of the Duma, and again used the army and bureaucracy to rule Russia.

cards.title: Model answer: Britain and France, 1850–1914
cards.problem: (Short answer) Compare political developments in Britain and France between 1850 and 1914.

steps.text: Britain – stability: it avoided revolution in 1848 thanks to reform (1832 law widening male suffrage) and economic growth.
Britain – parties: a two-party system (Liberals and Conservatives) by 1871, a Labour party by 1900; by 1918 all men over 21 and women over 30 could vote.
France – empire: Louis-Napoleon, elected president in 1848, became Emperor Napoleon III in 1852 after a plebiscite.
France – republic: his empire collapsed after the Franco-Prussian War; the Third Republic got a constitution in 1875.

cards.answer: Britain reformed gradually and stayed stable, while France moved from the Second Empire of Napoleon III to the Third Republic after defeat by Prussia.

lessons.title: Nationalism and Civil War in the United States

cards.title: Nationalism and Civil War in the United States
body: United States national unity was not achieved easily after the adoption of the Constitution. Two factions fought about the division of power in the new government.

The Federalists favored a strong central government. The Republicans, fearing central power, wanted the federal government to be subordinate to the state governments. These early divisions came to an end with the War of 1812 against the British.
By the mid-19th century, the issue of American national unity had reemerged. Slavery had become a threat to that unity.

Although the importation of slaves was banned in 1808, there were four million African American slaves in the South by 1860. The South’s economy was based on growing cotton on plantations, mostly by slave labor.
Thus abolitionism, a movement to end slavery, arose in the North and challenged the slavery in the South.

When the anti-slavery politician, Abraham Lincoln was elected president in November 1860, South Carolina decided to secede from the United States. In February 1861, six more Southern states did the same
And a rival state called the Confederate States of America was formed. In April, fighting erupted between the North and South.

Over 600,000 soldiers died during the war. The Union, with more men and resources, gradually weakened the Confederacy. With the surrender of Confederate forces on April 9, 1865, the unity of the United States was restored.

In 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution was passed. The amendment abolished slavery in the US. The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments gave citizenship to African Americans and the right to vote to African American males.

By the end of the 19th century, the United States began to expand abroad. The Samoan Islands in the Pacific became the first important United States colony. Hawaii was annexed by the United States in 1898.

In the same year, the United States also defeated Spain in the Spanish-American War. As a result, the United States acquired the formerly Spanish possessions of Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines.

cards.title: CANADA – The Emergence of a Settlers Nation in Canada
body: By the Treaty of Paris in 1763, signed at the end of the Seven Years ’War, Canada passed from the French to the British.
The indigenous people demanded independence However; there were also differences among the colonists.
In 1840, the British Parliament formally joined Upper and Lower Canada into the United Provinces of Canada.
In 1867, however, the British allowed the establishment of a Canadian state (the Dominion of Canada) with its own constitution.
Thus, Canada abolished a parliamentary system and ruled itself, although foreign affairs remained in the hands of the British government.

cards.title: Model answer: the American Civil War
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the causes and results of the American Civil War (1861–65).

steps.text: Cause – slavery: by 1860 there were four million slaves in the South, whose cotton economy depended on them; abolitionism grew in the North.
Trigger: Lincoln's election (November 1860) led South Carolina and six more states to secede and form the Confederacy.
War: fighting began in April 1861; over 600,000 soldiers died; the Union, with more men and resources, won (surrender 9 April 1865).
Results: national unity restored; the 13th Amendment abolished slavery, the 14th and 15th gave citizenship and the vote to African American men.

cards.answer: Slavery divided North and South; Lincoln's election led to secession and war, which the Union won in 1865, restoring unity and abolishing slavery.

cards.title: The Working Classes Movement
body: In the 1870s many workers made movements and protests against the industrial governments their main reasons were:
The desire to improve their working and living conditions.
Most of workers blamed the industrialist for the miserable working conditions.

Many workers organization were influenced and motivated by the works of KARL MAARX and FREDRICH ENGLES on the book of communist manifesto written in 1848.both writers favored socialism from industrial capitalism.
Marx believed that all of world history was a history of class struggles. Which encouraged class struggle for class less society led by workers and proletariats.
He also believed that that the final revolution would ultimately produce a classless society. The state (which had been an instrument of the bourgeois interests) would wither away.
Because of the ideas many socialist party grew some of them even overcome the government’s opposition example, the SOCIAL DEMOCRATIC PARTY OF GERMANY ,

In 1889, leaders of the various socialist parties from different countries joined together and formed an association of national socialist groups that would fight against capitalism worldwide. This association was called the Second International. (The First International had failed in 1872.)

cards.title: Completing these points: Marx, socialist parties and trade unions
body: **Why workers organized after 1870.** They wanted better working and living conditions and blamed the industrialists for their misery.

**The theory.** *The Communist Manifesto* was published in **1848** by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. History is a history of class struggle; the proletariat would overthrow the bourgeoisie, and a classless society would follow in which the state would "wither away".

**Socialist parties.** The **German Social Democratic Party (SPD)** was founded in 1875; despite government efforts to destroy it, it won four million votes in 1912 and became the largest party in Germany. Socialist parties appeared in other countries too.
**Trade unions.** British unions won the right to strike in the 1870s; by 1914 unions across Europe had improved working and living conditions.
**Second International (1889).** An international association of socialist parties against capitalism; the First International had failed in 1872.
**Memory trick:** "1848 Manifesto, 1875 SPD, 1889 Second International."

cards.title: 3.4.4 International Rivalry
body: Many European nations entered into different alliances such as:
Germany’s chief rival was France. To isolate France, Bismarck made an alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879. In 1882, Italy joined this alliance (the triple alliance). .

At the same time, Bismarck maintained a separate treaty with Russia and tried to remain on good terms with Great Britain. In 1890 Emperor William 2nd dismissed Bismarck from office for been too diplomatic.
By 1907, an alliance of Great Britain, France, and Russia known as the Triple Entente was formed.
Thus, Europe was divided into two opposing camps. By the beginning of 1914, these camps viewed each other with suspicion. This, among others causes, led to the First World War.

cards.title: Completing this point: how Europe split into two armed camps
body: **Step 1 – Germany isolates France.** After 1871 Germany was the strongest state and France its chief rival. Bismarck allied with Austria-Hungary (1879); Italy joined in 1882, forming the **Triple Alliance**.
**Step 2 – Bismarck's safety net.** He kept a separate treaty with Russia and stayed friendly with Britain.
**Step 3 – William II changes course.** He dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and ended the treaty with Russia.
**Step 4 – France and Russia join (1894).** They formed a military alliance.
**Step 5 – Britain joins them.** Fear of growing German power pushed Britain towards France, and by 1907 Britain, France and Russia formed the **Triple Entente**.
**Result.** Two suspicious camps by 1914 – one of the causes of the First World War.
**Memory trick:** "Alliance = G-A-I (Germany, Austria, Italy); Entente = B-F-R (Britain, France, Russia)."

cards.title: Model answer: the working-class movement
cards.problem: (Exam question) Why did a working-class movement develop in the late 19th century and what ideas guided it?

steps.text: Causes: workers wanted to improve their working and living conditions and blamed industrialists for miserable conditions.
Ideas: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels (The Communist Manifesto) taught that history is the history of class struggle between bourgeoisie and proletariat.
Goal: a workers' revolution leading to a classless society in which the state would wither away.
Organisation: socialist parties such as Germany's Social Democratic Party, and the Second International (1889).

cards.answer: Bad conditions led workers to organise; guided by Marx and Engels' idea of class struggle, they formed socialist parties and the Second International.

cards.title: Western Society, Culture and Science 1850-1914
body: 3.5.1 Society: different changes occurred in society
The Growth of Cities and the Social Structure.
The improvement of living conditions also enabled cities to grow faster in the second half of the nineteenth century.

By 1900, Europe was divided into two economic zones. Great Britain, Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Germany, the western part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and northern Italy made up an advanced industrialized areas. The remaining parts of Europe, i.e. Southern Italy, most of Austria-Hungary, Spain, Portugal, the Balkans, and Russia were mostly agricultural. The Movement for Women’s Rights
The massive industrialization of the late 19th century opened the door to new jobs for women.

cards.title: 3.5.2 Science and Scientific Ideas
body: The Scientific Revolution created a rational approach to the study of the natural world. The Industrial Revolution increased interest in scientific research.
The first major change in industry between 1870 and 1914 was the substitution of steel for iron.
In Great Britain, Michael Faraday put together a primitive generator that laid the foundation for the use of electricity.
By 1910, hydroelectric and coal-fired generator enabled homes and factories to be tied to a single, common source of power.
The creation of the light bulb by Thomas Edison in the United States.
A revolution in communications began when Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone in 1876 and Guglielmo Marconi invented the radio in 1901.
In 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright invented a fixed-wing plane with help of the new engine. In 1919, the first regular passenger air service was established.
In 1859, Charles Darwin published his ground-breaking major work, On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection.
The French scientist, Marie Curie. Discovered that an element called radium gave energy, or radiation, that came from within the atom itself.

cards.title: The cultural developments
body: Many cultural developments also took place such as

Romanticism: The Romantics believed that emotion and sentiment were only understandable to the person experiencing them. Romantics also valued individualism, the belief in the uniqueness of each person.

Realism: The belief that the world should be viewed realistically was closely related to science. Realism, however, also became a movement in the literary and visual arts. The literary Realists of the mid-19th.

Modernism: Between 1870 and 1914, many writers and artists rejected the traditional literary and artistic styles that had dominated European cultural life since the Renaissance. The changes that they produced was called Modernism.

Impressionism was a movement that began in France in the 1870s, when a group of artists rejected the studios where artists had traditionally worked and went out into the countryside to paint nature directly.
One of the most important figures in modern art was Pablo Picasso. He was from Spain but settled in Paris in 1904. He created a new style called Cubism.

cards.problem: (Short answer) Describe the main scientific and technological advances of 1850–1914.

steps.text: Industry: steel replaced iron.
Energy: Faraday's primitive generator laid the foundation for electricity; Edison created the light bulb.
Communications and transport: Bell's telephone (1876), Marconi's radio, the Wright brothers' aeroplane (1903).
Science: Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) and Marie Curie's work on radium.

cards.answer: Steel, electricity, the telephone, radio and aeroplane transformed life, while Darwin and Curie changed scientific thinking.

Great Britain was able to avoid the Revolution in 1848. In the beginning of 19th century, Great Britain was governed by aristocratic landowning classes, which dominated both houses of Parliament.

cards.front: How Did the Industrial Revolution Impact Society?
cards.back: Although the Industrial Revolution occurred approximately 200 years ago, it is a period that left a profound impact on how people lived and the way businesses operated.
The Industrial Revolution created an increase in employment opportunities. This led to significant improvements in city planning.
It led to a shortage of food production.
In the first half of the 19th century, the difficult conditions created by the Industrial Revolution gave rise to a movement known as Socialism.
